title: Chapter 27
paragraphs: After the grammar teacher's lesson came his father's lesson. While he waited for his father, Seryozha sat at the table playing with a penknife and slipped into a daydream. One of his favorite things to do was to look for his mother on his walks. He didn't really believe in death in general, and certainly not in her death — in spite of what Lidia Ivanovna had told him and his father had confirmed — and it was precisely because of that, and after they had told him she was dead, that he had started looking for her whenever he went out. Every woman with a full, graceful figure and dark hair was his mother. At the sight of such a woman, such a wave of tenderness rose in him that his breath caught and tears came to his eyes. And he was on tiptoe with expectation that she would walk up to him, lift her veil — and her whole face would be visible, she would smile, she would hug him, he would catch her scent, feel the softness of her arms, and cry with happiness, just the way he had one evening lying in her lap while she tickled him, and he laughed and bit her white fingers covered with rings. Later, when he found out by accident from his old nurse that his mother was not dead, and his father and Lidia Ivanovna had explained to him that she was dead to him because she was wicked (which he simply could not believe, because he loved her), he went on looking and waiting for her in the same way. That day in the public gardens there had been a lady in a lilac veil whom he had watched with a pounding heart, sure it was her as she came toward them along the path. The lady hadn't come up to them — she had vanished somewhere. That day, more intensely than ever, Seryozha felt a rush of love for her, and now, waiting for his father, he forgot everything else and cut all the way around the edge of the table with his penknife, staring straight ahead with shining eyes and daydreaming about her.
"Here's your papa!" said Vassily Lukitch, snapping him out of it.
Seryozha jumped up and went over to his father, kissed his hand, and looked at him intently, trying to spot signs of pleasure at the Alexander Nevsky.

"Did you have a nice walk?" said Alexey Alexandrovitch, settling into his easy chair, pulling the volume of the Old Testament toward him, and opening it. Although Alexey Alexandrovitch had told Seryozha more than once that every Christian should know Bible history thoroughly, he often consulted the Bible himself during the lesson, and Seryozha noticed it.

"Yes, it was very nice, papa," said Seryozha, sitting sideways on his chair and rocking it, which was against the rules. "I saw Nadinka" (Nadinka was a niece of Lidia Ivanovna's who was being brought up in her house). "She told me you'd been given a new star. Are you glad, papa?"

"First of all, please don't rock your chair," said Alexey Alexandrovitch. "And secondly, it isn't the reward that matters, but the work itself. I wish you'd understand that. If you take up your work, your studies, in order to win a reward, the work will seem hard to you; but when you work" — and Alexey Alexandrovitch, as he spoke, thought about how sense of duty had carried him through the dreary labor of the morning, which had consisted of signing one hundred and eighty papers — "loving your work, you will find your reward in the work itself."

Seryozha's eyes, which had been bright with cheerfulness and affection, went dull and dropped before his father's gaze. This was the same long-familiar tone his father always took with him, and Seryozha had learned by now to fall in with it. His father always talked to him — so Seryozha felt — as if he were addressing some imaginary boy, one of those boys who exist in books and are nothing like himself. So with his father Seryozha always tried to play the part of the storybook boy.
"You understand that, I hope?" said his father.
"Yes, papa," answered Seryozha, playing the imaginary boy.

The lesson was to learn by heart several verses from the Gospel and to recite the opening of the Old Testament. The verses from the Gospel Seryozha knew fairly well, but at the moment he was saying them he became so absorbed in watching the sharp, bony ridge of his father's forehead that he lost the thread, and he muddled the end of one verse with the beginning of another. So Alexey Alexandrovitch could tell he didn't understand what he was saying, and that irritated him.

He frowned and began explaining something Seryozha had heard many times and could never remember, because he understood it far too well — the same way that "suddenly" is an adverb of manner of action. Seryozha looked at his father with frightened eyes and could think only of whether his father would make him repeat what had just been said, as he sometimes did. And the thought so alarmed Seryozha that he now understood nothing at all. But his father did not make him repeat it, and moved on to the lesson from the Old Testament. Seryozha recounted the events themselves well enough, but when he was asked what certain events prefigured, he knew nothing, even though he had already been punished over this particular lesson. The passage at which he could not say a word, and started fidgeting and slicing at the table and rocking his chair, was where he was supposed to recite the patriarchs before the Flood. He didn't know a single one of them except Enoch, who had been taken up alive into heaven. Last time he had remembered their names, but now he had forgotten them completely — mainly because Enoch was his favorite person in the whole Old Testament, and Enoch being carried up to heaven was tied in his head to a long chain of thought, and he sank into that thought now while he stared, transfixed, at his father's watch-chain and a half-undone button on his waistcoat.

Seryozha utterly disbelieved in death, which they talked to him about so often. He didn't believe the people he loved could die, and above all that he himself would die. That was something completely unthinkable, impossible for him. But he had been told that everyone dies; he had even asked people he trusted, and they had confirmed it; his old nurse had said the same, though unwillingly. But Enoch hadn't died, so it followed that not everyone died. "And why can't someone else serve God like that and be taken up alive into heaven?" thought Seryozha. Bad people — meaning people Seryozha didn't like — they could die, but the good ones might all be like Enoch.
"Well, what are the names of the patriarchs?"
"Enoch, Enos —"

"You've said that already. This is bad, Seryozha, very bad. If you don't try to learn what is more necessary than anything for a Christian," said his father, getting up, "whatever can interest you? I am displeased with you, and Piotr Ignatitch" (this was the most important of his teachers) "is displeased with you.... I shall have to punish you."

His father and his teacher were both displeased with Seryozha, and he really did learn his lessons very badly. But he was not a stupid boy. On the contrary, he was far cleverer than the boys his teacher held up to him as examples. In his father's opinion, he didn't want to learn what he was being taught. In reality he couldn't learn it. He couldn't, because the claims of his own soul were more compelling to him than the claims his father and his teacher made on him. The two sets of claims were in conflict, and he was in direct opposition to his education. He was nine years old; he was a child; but he knew his own soul, it was precious to him, he guarded it the way the eyelid guards the eye, and without the key of love he let no one inside it. His teachers complained that he wouldn't learn, while his soul was brimming over with thirst for knowledge. And he was learning — from Kapitonitch, from his nurse, from Nadinka, from Vassily Lukitch — just not from his teachers. The stream his father and his teachers were counting on to turn their mill-wheels had long since dried up at the source, but its waters were doing their work in a different channel.

His father punished Seryozha by not letting him go visit Nadinka, Lidia Ivanovna's niece; but the punishment turned out happily for Seryozha. Vassily Lukitch was in a good mood and showed him how to make windmills. The whole evening went by on this project, and on dreaming about how to build a windmill he could ride on himself — grabbing onto the sails or strapping himself in and spinning round. Seryozha did not think about his mother all evening, but once he was in bed he suddenly remembered her, and in his own words he prayed that his mother, for his birthday tomorrow, would stop hiding herself and come to him.
"Vassily Lukitch, do you know what extra thing I prayed for tonight, besides the usual?"
"That you'd learn your lessons better?"
"No."
"Toys?"
"No. You'll never guess. A splendid thing — but it's a secret! When it happens, I'll tell you. Can't you guess?"
"No, I can't guess. Tell me yourself," said Vassily Lukitch with a smile, which was rare with him. "Come on, lie down, I'm putting out the candle."
"Without the candle I can see better what I see and what I prayed for. There — I almost gave away the secret!" said Seryozha, laughing happily.

When the candle was taken away, Seryozha heard and felt his mother. She was standing over him, caressing him with loving eyes. But then came windmills, a knife, everything began to mix together, and he fell asleep.
